The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\ne\{0\}$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space. Use the predual $M_*=Q$ of [[lem-qsmx-von-neumann-predual]]; its elements are the normal linear functionals, and the induced topology $\sigma(M,Q)$ is the ultraweak topology. A **normal state** on $M$ is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:M\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(I)=1$, $\omega(a)\geq0$ for every positive $a\in M$, and
$$\omega\!\left(\sup_i a_i\right)=\sup_i\omega(a_i)$$
for every increasing net $(a_i)$ of positive elements with $0\leq a_i\leq C I$ for a common finite $C$ and supremum taken in $M$.
An automorphism of $M$ is **normal** when it preserves the suprema of all such bounded increasing positive nets.
A **point-ultraweakly continuous one-parameter automorphism group** is a family $(\alpha_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ of bijective unital complex-linear maps $M\to M$ preserving multiplication and adjoints, with $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_M$, $\alpha_s\alpha_t=\alpha_{s+t}$, and $t\mapsto\varphi(\alpha_t(x))$ continuous for every $x\in M$ and every normal linear functional $\varphi\in Q$.
For dimensionless $t$ and dimensionless $\beta>0$, the normal state $\omega$ satisfies the **upper-strip $(\alpha,\beta)$ KMS condition** when, for every $A,B\in M$, there is a bounded scalar function $F_{A,B}$ on $S_\beta=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq\beta\}$ that is continuous on $S_\beta$, holomorphic in its interior, and satisfies
$$F_{A,B}(t)=\omega(A\alpha_t(B)),\qquad F_{A,B}(t+i\beta)=\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)\quad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

The rescaled maps satisfy
$\widetilde\alpha_{\tau_1}\widetilde\alpha_{\tau_2}
=\alpha_{\tau_1/\lambda+\tau_2/\lambda}
=\widetilde\alpha_{\tau_1+\tau_2}$ and
$\widetilde\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_M$. For each $X\in M$ and normal
linear functional $\varphi$, the map
$\tau\mapsto\varphi(\widetilde\alpha_\tau(X))
=\varphi(\alpha_{\tau/\lambda}(X))$ is continuous because it is the
composition of the continuous map $t\mapsto\varphi(\alpha_t(X))$ with
$\tau\mapsto\tau/\lambda$. Thus $\widetilde\alpha$ is a
point-ultraweakly continuous one-parameter group.

For each $A,B\in M$, choose the strip function $F_{A,B}$ supplied by
[F1] and define $G_{A,B}(z)=F_{A,B}(z/\lambda)$. Since $\lambda>0$, the
map $z\mapsto z/\lambda$ sends the closed strip of width $\lambda\theta$
bijectively to $S_\theta$ and its interior to the interior. Therefore
$G_{A,B}$ is bounded and continuous on the closed rescaled strip and
holomorphic inside.

For real $\tau$, the boundaries are
$G_{A,B}(\tau)=\omega(A\alpha_{\tau/\lambda}(B))
=\omega(A\widetilde\alpha_\tau(B))$ and
$G_{A,B}(\tau+i\lambda\theta)
=\omega(\alpha_{\tau/\lambda}(B)A)
=\omega(\widetilde\alpha_\tau(B)A)$. These are precisely the required
upper-strip boundary values at width $\lambda\theta$.

boundaries.reason: The statement assumes a nonzero unital von Neumann algebra and quantifies over its elements.
The hypotheses require theta>0 and lambda>0; zero strip width or zero rescaling is excluded.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 2.1 remain valid at lambda=1, where the parameter and strip width are unchanged.
Steps 1.1–2.1 do not require a nontrivial automorphism group; they also apply to the identity group and to a one-dimensional algebra when the stated KMS functions exist.
Steps 1.2–2.1 map the closed strip, including both boundary lines, and verify each boundary value.
The premise is explicit in A1; step 1.2 uses the supplied function separately for each fixed A,B and does not assert a uniform choice beyond the hypothesis.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For a spatial wave vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, with each component in
$\mathrm m^{-1}$ and the Euclidean norm, define
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}\in\mathbb R_{>0}$, with
unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here $\omega_\mu$ is the temporal wave number, not the
SI angular frequency; the corresponding SI angular frequency is
$c\omega_\mu$. Energy and momentum are $E=\hbar c\omega_\mu$ in joules and
$\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With
$p=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)\in\mathbb R^4$ and
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$, the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

For a selected local action represented on a chart region
$\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ by
$$\frac{S}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathcal U}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}(x)\,d^4x,\quad d^4x:=dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3,$$
the natural Lagrangian density $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ has unit
$\mathrm m^{-4}$. Since $x^0=ct$, the corresponding SI Lagrangian density is
$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{SI}}:=\hbar c\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ and has unit
$\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. This unit conversion alone does not identify a
Lagrangian density with the model's Hamiltonian energy density.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
use the formal field symbols $\phi_{\rm n}$ and $\psi_{\rm n}$ in the selected
scalar and Dirac kinetic terms, assigning them length degrees $-1$ and
$-3/2$, respectively. These are the dimensions fixed by those free kinetic
terms, not exact scaling dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous
dimensions, when present, are separate quantities. These symbols do not
assert pointwise field maps or operator fields; a model supplies its field
space and regularity. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

In a supplied four-component spinor representation, let
$\gamma^a\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C^4)$, $a=0,1,2,3$, be
dimensionless linear maps satisfying
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}:=\gamma^a\gamma^b+\gamma^b\gamma^a
=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$, where $I_4$ is the identity map. Set $\beta:=\gamma^0$
and $\alpha^i:=\beta\gamma^i$; then $\beta^2=I_4$ and
$\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$. For a supplied four-component spinor $\psi$ write
$\bar\psi:=\psi^\dagger\beta$. The effective Clifford metric is $-\eta$.
A supplied free Dirac model may use
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$ for its model-supplied spinor field
$\psi$; that model supplies its field domain and regularity. The phase and
Clifford choices are conventions; this item proves no representation or field
equation.

For the autonomous evolution convention, assume Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]]: every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice
function. Let a selected model supply a complex Hilbert space $\mathscr H$
as in [[def-hilbert-space]] and a time-independent complex-linear Hamiltonian
$H:D(H)\to\mathscr H$ with a specified dense linear domain
$D(H)\subseteq\mathscr H$ and SI energy
unit joules. Require self-adjointness as in
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]: $H=H^*$,
including equality of domains and values. Here $y\in D(H^*)$ precisely when
there is a $z\in\mathscr H$ such that
$\langle Hx,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every $x\in D(H)$, and
$H^*y=z$; density makes $z$ unique.

The published mathematical supplier
[[lem-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-cc-arbitrary-hilbert-spectral-calculus]]
then supplies the spectral measure $E_H$ on the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R$. This is a normalized projection-valued measure as in
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]: its values are bounded orthogonal
projections, $E_H(\mathbb R)=I$, $E_H(B\cap C)=E_H(B)E_H(C)$, and it is
countably additive in norm on every vector. For $\xi\in\mathscr H$ put
$\nu_\xi(B):=\langle E_H(B)\xi,\xi\rangle$, a finite positive measure.
The spectral integral of $\lambda$ represents $H$, on exactly the domain
$D(H)=\{\xi\in\mathscr H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,d\nu_\xi(\lambda)<\infty\}$.
For real $t$ in seconds define the autonomous evolution by bounded Borel
functional calculus,
$$U(t):=\exp(-itH/\hbar):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda).$$
The spectral variable $\lambda$ carries unit joule. This exponential is a
bounded operator on all of $\mathscr H$, even when $H$ is unbounded; it
does not mean an operator power series on arbitrary vectors. The supplier
gives a strongly continuous unitary group: $U(0)=I$,
$U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$ and $\|U(t)\xi-U(t_0)\xi\|\to0$ as $t\to t_0$ for
each $\xi\in\mathscr H$. A model may restrict it to a declared
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$. Each $U(t)$ is a surjective complex-linear map
satisfying $\langle U(t)\xi,U(t)\zeta\rangle=\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle$
for all $\xi,\zeta\in\mathscr H$; write $U(t)^*:=U(t)^{-1}$. The exponent
is dimensionless because $\hbar$ has unit $\mathrm{J\,s}$. For any
model-supplied complex-linear operator $O:D(O)\to\mathscr H$, with specified
linear domain $D(O)\subseteq\mathscr H$, define its Heisenberg conjugate by
$$O_H(t):=U(t)^*O\,U(t),\quad D(O_H(t)):=\{\xi\in\mathscr H:U(t)\xi\in D(O)\}.$$
The model supplies the Hamiltonian and operator domains; the spectral supplier
justifies this evolution only for those data and hypotheses. This dictionary
constructs no model-specific Hamiltonian or field representation and does not
adopt a physical dynamics law. Where a free-field
module uses an inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the
repository's first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction. It
asserts only matrix-element continuity and the stated linear maps; all further
operator properties, locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior must be supplied by a constructed
model. Test-function units can be chosen so a specified smeared observable is
dimensionless; there is no universal test-function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. Identify parenthesizations by the isometry fixing
elementary tensors: the product pairing is the same on their dense span,
so the map and its inverse extend to the completions. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $h\in H$, the map $C_h:H\to\mathbb C$, $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$, is linear and bounded:
$|C_h(v)|=|(v,h)_1|\le\|h\|\,\|v\|$ by
[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]].
For any Hilbert space $K$, identify $\mathbb C\widehat\otimes K$ with $K$
by $J_K(z\otimes v)=zv$. Every algebraic tensor is $1\otimes w$;
the tensor norm is then $\|w\|$, so $J_K$ extends to a surjective isometry
on the completion (with inverse $w\mapsto1\otimes w$).
Throughout the following formulas, $C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)}$ means
$J_{H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}}\circ(C_h\widehat\otimes I)$, with
$I$ the identity on $H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}$.
The bounded tensor-map supplier therefore applies and gives norm at most
$\|h\|$. This includes $n=1$, where $H^{\widehat\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.
Contraction commutes with permutations of the remaining $n-1$ factors,
so it takes symmetric or antisymmetric tensors to the corresponding
$(n-1)$-particle sector (and to $\mathbb C$ for $n=1$).

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h$ is the bounded functional above, its tensor extension is supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Fix four-dimensional affine Minkowski spacetime with metric
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, an inertial length-coordinate chart
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$, $x^0=ct$, and coordinates measured in metres, as specified
by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Write
$\Box=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$. The mass-shell parameter $\mu\ge0$ has
unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same unit. For a
massive species, $\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c/\hbar$; $\mu=0$ is the separately
admitted massless branch of the mathematical free-field construction. Thus
$\hbar c\omega_\mu$ is physical energy and $\hbar\mathbf k$ is physical
momentum. The natural-unit action is written $S/\hbar$.

The scalar one-particle space is
$\mathcal H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C)$, where
$H_\mu^+=\{(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k):\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3,\ \omega_\mu(\mathbf k)>0\}$ and
$d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))$; at $\mu=0$ the
measure-zero apex $\mathbf k=0$ is omitted. These are the shell conventions
of [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]].

For a smooth real classical scalar $\phi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R$
with the canonical free-field length degree $-1$, adopt
$$\frac{S_\phi}{\hbar}=-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi_{\mathrm n}\partial_b\phi_{\mathrm n}+\mu^2\phi_{\mathrm n}^2\right)\,d^4x.$$
For a smooth commuting classical Dirac spinor
$\psi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb C^4$ with canonical free-field length
degree $-3/2$, put $\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}=\psi_{\mathrm n}^\dagger\beta$ and
use the Clifford convention
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ from
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. Adopt
$$\frac{S_D}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}\,d^4x.$$
The smooth classical variables in these functionals commute; no Grassmann
algebra or path-integral construction is being adopted. These formulas specify
local action densities: for arbitrary smooth global fields the total
integrals need not converge. Only compactly supported variations are used;
the action difference under such a variation is an integral over a compact
set and is finite for smooth fields. With these variations on the fixed
background, the intended Euler–Lagrange equations are
$(\Box-\mu^2)\phi_{\mathrm n}=0$ and
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}=0$, conditional on the exact
mathematical supplier recorded as [L1] below.

As the physical interpretation of this selected free model, assign the real
scalar species to the bosonic symmetric Fock representation and assign the
Dirac field to the particle/antiparticle CAR representation on
$\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. Choose the zero-particle Fock
vectors as the scalar and Dirac vacuum states. This is an adopted species and
statistics assignment. The CCR/CAR and operator properties of the specified
representations are mathematical model consequences; they do not prove a
general spin-statistics theorem or establish that nature realizes this model.

The scalar construction is the Schwartz-smeared field
$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f)$ on the finite-particle
domain, with the future-shell phase
$p\circ x=\omega_\mu x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x$, exactly as in
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. The Dirac construction is the bounded
spacetime-smeared CAR field of
[[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]], using the positive and negative
projections of the specified free Dirac matrix. In that carrier,
$\mathcal H_D=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3;\mathbb C^4)$,
$h_D(\mathbf k)=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf k+\beta\mu$, and
$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=(I_4\pm h_D(\mathbf k)/\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))/2$; the
particle and antiparticle one-particle spaces are the closed ranges
$\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. These carriers state their
mathematical hypotheses and construction domains; their draft status is not an

Tong's lecture notes and Srednicki's book draft provide independent
presentations of the scalar and Dirac free-field formulations. Their formal
mode notation supplies context for this adoption, not a proof of the
operator-domain claims and not evidence that the adopted model describes
nature.

normalizations adopted in [[post-qft-free-field-model]]. For an open spacetime
region $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, a scalar test is a real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)$ and a Dirac test is a
$F\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb C^4)$. These are compactly supported smooth test
functions on the fixed inertial Minkowski chart.

For scalar tests use the bounded Weyl operators
$$W_\mu(f)=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f),$$
where $K_\mu$ is the future-shell restriction and
$W_{\rm Segal}$ is the unitary generated by the closed Segal field, with the
normalization and phase convention of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. Define the scalar bounded observable algebra
$\mathfrak A_s(O)$ to be the norm closure of the unital $*$-algebra generated
by these $W_\mu(f)$. The real smeared field is symmetric on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ and its self-adjoint closure has the exact multiplier
domain supplied by [[lem-qft-free-domain-observables]] and
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]].

For Dirac tests, $\Psi(F)$ is the bounded smeared CAR field of
[[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]]. Define $\mathfrak A_D(O)$ as the norm
closure of the unital algebra generated by products containing an even number
of these field operators and their adjoints, with all test supports in $O$.
“Even” here means even field parity, or equivalently an even number of odd
CAR field generators in each product. The even algebra is the selected local
Dirac observable algebra; an odd charged field is not included as a commuting
local observable.

The selected vacuum states on bounded operators are the vector states
$\omega_s(A)=\langle\Omega_s,A\Omega_s\rangle$ and
$\omega_D(B)=\langle\Omega_D,B\Omega_D\rangle$. For the scalar Fock space,
define the total number, Hamiltonian, and physical momentum components by
$$N_s=d\Gamma_s(1),\qquad H_s=\hbar c\,d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu),\qquad P_{s,j}=\hbar\,d\Gamma_s(k_j).$$
Here $d\Gamma_s$ acts on the $n$-particle sector by summing the displayed
one-particle multiplier over its $n$ arguments. Their maximal domains are
the square-integrability domains of those sector sums; in particular,
$$D(N_s)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
These physical components have one-particle momentum $+\hbar k_j$, as in
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. The mathematical spatial generators in
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] and [[lem-qft-free-domain-observables]] use
$G_{s,j}=d\Gamma_s(-k_j)$ with the positive-exponent convention;
thus $P_{s,j}=-\hbar G_{s,j}$. For a translation increment
$a=(a^0,\mathbf a)$ in length coordinates, the scalar translation unitary
is the sectorwise phase
$\exp(i(a^0H_s/(\hbar c)-\sum_j a^jP_{s,j}/\hbar))$.
Changing the sign does not change the maximal domain, since the squared
sector multiplier is unchanged. This also follows directly from
[[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]] with multiplier $k_j$. For the Dirac Fock space, let $H$
and $P_j$ be the mathematical translation generators of
[[lem-qft-dirac-fermionic-translation-spectrum]]. Their one-particle
multipliers are respectively $(\omega_\mu,\mathbf k)$ for particles and
$(\omega_\mu,-\mathbf k)$ for antiparticles, and the sector multiplier is
their sum. Define the physical Dirac Hamiltonian and momentum by
$H_D=\hbar cH$ and $P_{D,j}=\hbar P_j$, using the positive SI constants from
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. Their exact domains are unchanged by these
nonzero scale factors; their multipliers have units joules and momentum,
respectively.

For any of these self-adjoint operators $A$, a normalized state
$\Psi\in D(A)$ has model mean $\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle$ and variance
$\operatorname{Var}_\Psi(A)=\|(A-\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle)\Psi\|^2$.
This requires the second spectral moment but does not require
$\Psi\in D(A^2)$. Products of unbounded operators use their composition
domains.

If a signed charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}\in\mathbb R$ measured in coulombs is supplied, the intended
Dirac charge-number operator is $Q_{\rm SI}=q_{\rm SI}(N_p-N_{\bar p})$.
Here $\Pi_p$ and $\Pi_{\bar p}$ are the orthogonal projections onto
$\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$; on the $n$-particle sector,
$N_p$ and $N_{\bar p}$ are the sums of the corresponding projections over
the $n$ tensor factors. Its candidate maximal direct-sum domain is
$$D(Q_{\rm SI})=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge0}\left\|q_{\rm SI}\sum_{r=1}^n(\Pi_p-\Pi_{\bar p})^{(r)}\Psi_n\right\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
This is a candidate definition only; no self-adjointness or proved-domain
claim is asserted here.

Measurements in this model are assigned only when a state and a normalized
finite bounded Kraus instrument have actually been constructed. For such an
instrument, the adopted outcome probabilities and positive-probability
conditional states are exactly those of
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]]. They are model probabilities,
not observed outcomes. The field definitions are test-smeared: neither
$\Phi_\mu(x)$ nor $\Psi(x)$ is a pointwise operator supplied here, and the
smearing results do not define coincident products or a diagonal restriction.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is
$$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$
understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback
and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock
lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
and for the bounded Weyl operators.

For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the
second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector
$(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed
future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector
at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions.
No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume both the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Fix a
massive real scalar species with rest mass $m_{\mathrm{rest}}>0$ in kilograms.
Use four-dimensional affine Minkowski spacetime with metric
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and length coordinates
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, where $x^0=ct$ and $c>0$ has units
$\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Set $\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest}}c/\hbar>0$ in
$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, where $\hbar>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. The future shell,
one-particle space, and measure are
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p):(p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\},\qquad \mathcal H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu),\qquad d\nu_\mu=\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3\,2\sqrt{|\mathbf p|^2+\mu^2}}.$$
Take the scalar Hilbert space to be the bosonic symmetric Fock space
$\mathcal H=\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_\mu)$ and its unit zero-particle vector
to be $\Omega$.

For an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ and real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)$, define
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x, \qquad W_\mu(f)=W_{\mathrm{Segal}}(\sqrt2\,K_\mu f).$$
Let $\mathfrak A_s(O)$ be the operator-norm closure of the unital
$*$-algebra generated by all these bounded Weyl unitaries, and set
$W_R=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x^1>|x^0|\}$ and
$M(W_R)=\mathfrak A_s(W_R)''\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. Here
$\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ denotes the bounded linear operators;
$\mathcal S'$ is the set of bounded operators commuting with every member of
$\mathcal S$, and $\mathcal S''=(\mathcal S')'$. Thus $M(W_R)$ is a concrete
von Neumann algebra in the chosen double-commutant convention.

For dimensionless rapidity $s\in\mathbb R$, define the future-directed boost
by
$$\Lambda_W(s)(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3) =(x^0\cosh s+x^1\sinh s,\ x^0\sinh s+x^1\cosh s,\ x^2,\ x^3).$$
Use its scalar Fock implementation: on the one-particle space
$[u_\mu(\Lambda)\psi](p)=\psi(\Lambda^{-1}p)$, and on the $n$-particle
symmetric sector $U(\Lambda)=u_\mu(\Lambda)^{\otimes_s n}$, with the vacuum
sector fixed. The QFT Fock pairing is linear in its second argument; for the
modular definitions use the equivalent first-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_1:=\langle v,u\rangle_2$. Thus the vacuum vector state
is $\omega_W(X)=\langle X\Omega,\Omega\rangle_1

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume both the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Fix a
massive real scalar species with rest mass $m_{\mathrm{rest}}>0$ in kilograms.
Use four-dimensional affine Minkowski spacetime with metric
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and length coordinates
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, where $x^0=ct$ and $c>0$ has units
$\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Set $\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest}}c/\hbar>0$ in
$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, where $\hbar>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. The future shell,
one-particle space, and measure are
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p):(p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\},\qquad \mathcal H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu),\qquad d\nu_\mu=\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3\,2\sqrt{|\mathbf p|^2+\mu^2}}.$$
Take the scalar Hilbert space to be the bosonic symmetric Fock space
$\mathcal H=\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_\mu)$ and its unit zero-particle vector
to be $\Omega$.

For an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ and real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)$, define
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x, \qquad W_\mu(f)=W_{\mathrm{Segal}}(\sqrt2\,K_\mu f).$$
Let $\mathfrak A_s(O)$ be the operator-norm closure of the unital
$*$-algebra generated by all these bounded Weyl unitaries, and set
$W_R=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x^1>|x^0|\}$ and
$M(W_R)=\mathfrak A_s(W_R)''\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. Here
$\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ denotes the bounded linear operators;
$\mathcal S'$ is the set of bounded operators commuting with every member of
$\mathcal S$, and $\mathcal S''=(\mathcal S')'$. Thus $M(W_R)$ is a concrete
von Neumann algebra in the chosen double-commutant convention.

For dimensionless rapidity $s\in\mathbb R$, define the future-directed boost
by
$$\Lambda_W(s)(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3) =(x^0\cosh s+x^1\sinh s,\ x^0\sinh s+x^1\cosh s,\ x^2,\ x^3).$$
Use its scalar Fock implementation: on the one-particle space
$[u_\mu(\Lambda)\psi](p)=\psi(\Lambda^{-1}p)$, and on the $n$-particle
symmetric sector $U(\Lambda)=u_\mu(\Lambda)^{\otimes_s n}$, with the vacuum
sector fixed. The QFT Fock pairing is linear in its second argument; for the
modular definitions use the equivalent first-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_1:=\langle v,u\rangle_2$. Thus the vacuum vector state
is $\omega_W(X)=\langle X\Omega,\Omega\rangle_1
=\langle\Omega,X\Omega\rangle_2$. Assume explicitly that $\Omega$ is cyclic and separating for
$M(W_R)$, meaning $\overline{M(W_R)\Omega}=\mathcal H$ and
$X\Omega=0$ for $X\in M(W_R)$ implies $X=0$. The Tomita operator is the
closure of $S_{W,0}(X\Omega)=X^*\Omega$ on $M(W_R)\Omega$; write its polar
decomposition as $S_W=J_W\Delta_W^{1/2}$, in the standard modular-data
convention.

As an additional model interface, adopt
$$\Delta_W^{it}=U(\Lambda_W(-2\pi t))\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
This geometric identity and cyclic-separating property are explicit adopted
assumptions for this selected model. The abstract Tomita–Takesaki theorem
supplies modular automorphisms and their KMS property, but this carrier does
not use it as a proof that the modular unitaries equal spacetime boosts. No
tensor-product factorization of the continuum Hilbert space across the wedge
and its complement is assumed.

derivations.claim:
Let $\psi_{z,N}=\sqrt{1-z}\sum_{n=0}^N z^{n/2}
|n\rangle_R\otimes|n\rangle_L$. Orthogonality gives, for $M>N$,
$\|\psi_{z,M}-\psi_{z,N}\|^2=(1-z)\sum_{n=N+1}^M z^n
\le (1-z)\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}z^n=z^{N+1}\to0$.
Thus the partial sums converge in $\mathcal H_R\otimes\mathcal H_L$ to
$\psi_z$. Also $(1-z)\sum_{n=0}^N z^n=1-z^{N+1}$, so continuity of the
norm gives $\langle\psi_z|\psi_z\rangle
=(1-z)\sum_{n=0}^\infty z^n=1$.

The product-basis coefficients are
$\langle m,k|\psi_z\rangle=\sqrt{1-z}\,z^{k/2}\delta_{mk}$.
Substitution in the defining partial-trace sum gives
$\langle m|\rho_R|n\rangle
=(1-z)\sum_{k=0}^\infty z^k\delta_{mk}\delta_{nk}
=(1-z)z^n\delta_{mn}$. Therefore the eigenvalues are exactly
$p_n=(1-z)z^n$, they are positive, and their sum is one by step 1.1.

Put $a_n=nz^n$ for $n\ge1$. Since
$a_{n+1}/a_n=z(1+1/n)\to z<1$, choose $q$ with $z<q<1$; for all
sufficiently large $n$, $a_{n+1}\le q a_n$, so $a_n\to0$ and the tail
$\sum a_n$ is bounded by a geometric series. Differentiating
$\sum_{n=0}^N z^n=(1-z^{N+1})/(1-z)$ gives
$\sum_{n=1}^N n z^{n-1}
=\bigl(1-(N+1)z^N+Nz^{N+1}\bigr)/(1-z)^2$. Since $Nz^N\to0$,
taking $N\to\infty$ gives $\sum_{n=0}^\infty n z^n=z/(1-z)^2$. Hence
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty n p_n=z/(1-z)$, and
$-\sum_{n=0}^\infty p_n\ln p_n
=-\ln(1-z)-(\ln z)\sum_{n=0}^\infty n p_n
=-\ln(1-z)-z\ln z/(1-z)$. The series converges because
$\sum z^n$ and $\sum n z^n$ converge for $0<z<1$. In particular,
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty p_n|\ln p_n|
=|\ln(1-z)|+|\ln z|\,z/(1-z)<\infty$.

Step 2.1 shows that the coefficient formula in the Example gives
$\rho_R|n\rangle=p_n|n\rangle$ with $0<p_n<1$ and $\sum_n p_n=1$; hence
$\rho_R$ is bounded and nonzero. Step 1.1 gives $P_z\ne0$. Every element of
$V_z$ therefore has a unique form $cP_z$, so $\mathcal R_z(cP_z)=c\rho_R$
defines a linear map from $V_z$ to $W_z$. On $P_z$ its matrix coefficients
are exactly those of the rank-one coefficient formula in the Example; thus
$\mathcal R_z(P_z)=\rho_R$ and the displayed rank-one diagram commutes. The
asserted reduction is confined to this rank-one input. The continuum
postulate [F1] instead defines a scalar Fock representation and a right-wedge
von Neumann algebra; no map identifying those two constructions is defined
or used here. Consequently this example proves the stated oscillator
identities but no continuum wedge factorization or density-matrix claim.
